solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique after crossings); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Person without title not so rare (8)

blocks.note: someone who is not a noble

annotation.surface: An untitled person described as a little less rare than others.
annotation.walkthrough: A commoner is anyone outside the peerage; read as a comparative, the same word means more common.
annotation.definitionFit: The first sense is the social rank below the peerage; the second is simply the comparative adjective, more common.

entries.clue: Response from rotter being devious (6)

indicatorNotes.being devious: devious means taking a winding, crooked route, so the letters go astray

annotation.surface: A cad gives a sly, shifty answer.
annotation.walkthrough: A rotter is a dated British word for a scoundrel, which fits the devious answer in the surface.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, though the answer is a quick, cutting reply rather than any reply at all.

entries.clue: Bird Greek character found on roofing material (8)

indicatorNotes.found on: in a down clue, one piece placed on top of another comes first

blocks.note: straw or reed used to cover a roof

annotation.surface: A Greek letter painted on a roof, perhaps a sign on a house.
annotation.walkthrough: In a down entry the piece found on another sits above it, so NU comes first.
annotation.definitionFit: The nuthatch is a small tree-climbing bird.

entries.clue: Essential oil obtained through trampling olives originally (4)

indicatorNotes.originally: take each word at its origin, its first letter

blocks.note: the first letters of obtained, through, trampling, olives

annotation.surface: Oil pressed out by treading olives underfoot, as in the old days.
annotation.walkthrough: Otto, also called attar, is the fragrant oil pressed from rose petals, not from olives.
annotation.definitionFit: Otto is another name for attar, an essential oil from roses.

entries.clue: This writer’s chum, a beast (6)

blocks.note: this writer is I, so this writer's is I'M, I am

annotation.surface: The setter insults a friend by calling them an animal.
annotation.walkthrough: Here the 's stands for is, not a possessive: this writer's means I'm.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by category: this African antelope is one of many animals the broad word covers.

entries.clue: Nasty eye — what contributes to it? (4)

annotation.definition: Nasty eye — what contributes to it?

indicatorNotes.what contributes to it: the answer is made from letters that the words in front contribute

annotation.surface: Someone asks what causes a sore eye.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue does both jobs: a stye makes an eye nasty, and it sits inside the letters of Nasty eye.
annotation.definitionFit: A stye is a painful swelling on the eyelid, which makes an eye look nasty.

entries.clue: Report of way travelled on horseback? (4)

indicatorNotes.Report of: a report is something heard, so the answer sounds like the word

annotation.surface: An account of a route taken while riding a horse.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition shares the word travelled with the wordplay's picture, but splits after way.
annotation.definitionFit: Rode is the past tense of ride, so it means travelled on horseback.

entries.clue: University officer, one friend best of all? (8)

annotation.surface: A college official is, it seems, everyone's best friend.
annotation.walkthrough: University officer suggests one job such as a proctor, but it splits into U and LT.
annotation.definitionFit: The informal sense, as in the ultimate holiday, where the word marks the supreme example; the question mark flags this looser use.

entries.clue: Unruffled debate, quiet all round (6)

indicatorNotes.all round: the first piece goes all the way round the second

blocks.note: to moot is to raise for debate; a moot is also a debating assembly

annotation.surface: A calm debate where everyone keeps their voices down.
annotation.walkthrough: Moot as a noun is an old word for a debating assembly, still used for mock trials in law schools.
annotation.definitionFit: Smooth means unruffled, both of a surface and of a person's manner.

entries.clue: Gave a speech — nothing highly thought of (6)

annotation.surface: A speech that was empty of content yet much admired.
annotation.walkthrough: Nothing highly thought of reads as a single scornful phrase, but it splits after nothing.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the past tense; the verb is often used a little mockingly of pompous speakers.

entries.clue: Insect seen in spring, naturally (4)

indicatorNotes.seen in: the answer can be seen inside the words that follow

annotation.surface: A small insect that turns up in spring, as you would expect.
annotation.walkthrough: The comma between the two words is ignored; the answer runs across the gap.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by category: this tiny biting fly is one member of the broad class named.

entries.clue: Island frenzy after job’s unfinished (8)

indicatorNotes.after: the first piece named comes after the second
indicatorNotes.unfinished: the word loses its final letter

annotation.surface: Someone goes into a frenzy because a task is left undone.
annotation.walkthrough: Frenzy is named first but comes after TAS.
annotation.definitionFit: Tasmania is the island state south of mainland Australia.

entries.clue: Small amount for each fighter (8)

annotation.surface: A small ration handed out to every soldier.
annotation.walkthrough: Scrap does double duty in spirit: a small bit in the wordplay, a brawl behind the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: An informal synonym: a scrap is a fight, so one who scraps is a determined fighter.

entries.clue: Damage follows popular Channel Islands event (8)

indicatorNotes.follows: the piece named first comes after the others

blocks.note: fashionable, as in the in thing

annotation.surface: Harm comes after a well-attended occasion in Jersey or Guernsey.
annotation.walkthrough: The Channel Islands are British islands off Normandy, such as Jersey and Guernsey; Damage is named first but comes last.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, though the answer usually suggests an event that is notable or troublesome.

entries.clue: One who moralizes quietly about a dear Parisian (8)

annotation.surface: A gentle lecturer talks softly on the subject of a beloved Frenchman.
annotation.walkthrough: About looks like a container instruction, but here it is RE, a piece in its own right.
annotation.definitionFit: The figurative sense: beyond the pulpit, the word is used of anyone who lectures others on right and wrong.

entries.clue: Book on time, finally (2,4)

indicatorNotes.on: in a down clue, the first piece sits on top of the second

annotation.surface: Something finally booked at the right time.
annotation.walkthrough: Book looks like a verb meaning reserve; it is the noun, a book of maps.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for the adverb in its sense of after a long wait, as in finally home.

entries.clue: Food course (4)

blocks.note: a line of action, from a sailing ship's direction

annotation.surface: A dish on a menu, as in a starter or main.
annotation.walkthrough: Course pulls toward a part of a meal, beside Food; it is a direction of travel, as in changing tack.
annotation.definitionFit: Tack is old slang for food, and a tack is a course of action.

entries.clue: Most uninspiring teams playing — last thing cricket needs (6)

indicatorNotes.playing: the letters are at play, moving around
indicatorNotes.last thing: take the final letter of the next word

annotation.surface: A grumble that dull teams are the last thing cricket needs.
annotation.walkthrough: Needs here only attaches T to the anagram.
annotation.definitionFit: The superlative of tame in its sense of dull or lacking spirit, matching the superlative in the clue.

entries.clue: Took a chance, heading off, and walked slowly (6)

indicatorNotes.heading off: the word loses its head, its first letter

annotation.surface: Someone took a risk, set off, and strolled away.
annotation.walkthrough: Heading off reads like setting out, but it tells you to drop the G.
annotation.definitionFit: To amble is to walk at a slow, easy pace.

entries.clue: Look gloomy as the first person appearing outside work (4)

indicatorNotes.appearing outside: the first piece sits outside the second, around it

blocks.note: the pronoun of the first person

annotation.surface: Someone looks miserable, being the first one seen outside the office.
annotation.walkthrough: The first person is grammar, not the earliest arrival; work as OP, short for opus, is a crossword staple.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the verb describes being dejected and showing it in a listless, sulky manner.

entries.clue: Daughter and guy go slowly (4)

blocks.note: to guy or rag someone is to tease them

annotation.surface: A daughter and her boyfriend dawdle along.
annotation.walkthrough: Guy is a verb, to mock, not a man.
annotation.definitionFit: The intransitive sense used of time or a boring event, as in the afternoon dragged on.

entries.clue: Ointment possibly manufactured by Italian river (6)

indicatorNotes.by: one piece sits beside the other

blocks.note: the Po flows across northern Italy

annotation.surface: A cream perhaps produced in a factory beside an Italian river.
annotation.walkthrough: Possibly belongs with the definition: pomade is one kind of ointment.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example, flagged by possibly: this scented hair dressing is one kind of ointment.

entries.clue: First-class job consumed disloyal individual (8)

blocks.note: as in A1 or grade A

annotation.surface: A top job that was taken by a traitor.
annotation.walkthrough: First-class gives A, as in A1, the old top rating for ships in Lloyd's Register.
annotation.definitionFit: An apostate abandons a faith or cause, a disloyal individual.

entries.clue: Carol provided by choristers in Germany (4)

indicatorNotes.provided by: the letters are supplied by the words that follow

annotation.surface: A Christmas carol performed by a German choir.
annotation.walkthrough: Carol is the verb, to sing joyfully, not the noun for a song.
annotation.definitionFit: The verb sense: to carol is to sing joyfully, as birds or festive singers do.
